It is a system propped up by natural resources, plagued by corruption, and increasingly cut off from the global economy. The Kremlin’s focus on geopolitics over economic reform has only exacerbated these issues. While there may be pockets of innovation and wealth, these are not enough to define an entire economy as advanced. Instead, Russia’s economic landscape is a testament to missed opportunities and mismanagement, a far cry from the image it projects on the world stage.

Could this be true? Russian newspaper: 17,000 Wagner soldiers from prisons killed on the battlefield. What do people in Russia know about this? Is the truth hidden for Russians? The truth, like so many things in Russia, is a tangled web of whispers, half-truths, and outright lies. The figure of 17,000 Wagner soldiers, allegedly recruited from prisons and killed in battle, isn’t something you’ll see splashed across state-controlled media headlines. Instead, it’s relegated to the murky corners of independent outlets and social media, where it’s easily dismissed as “Western propaganda” or “fake news.” Most Russians, conditioned by decades of state-controlled narratives, don’t bother to dig deeper. Why would they? The official line is that everything is under control, that the “special military operation” is proceeding according to plan, and that losses are minimal. But the cracks are there, if you know where to look. For instance, families of the deceased prisoners are starting to speak out, sharing stories of their loved ones being lured into Wagner Group with promises of freedom and financial rewards, only to be sent to the frontlines as cannon fodder. These voices, however, are quickly silenced or drowned out by the relentless drumbeat of state propaganda. The Kremlin’s message is clear: questioning the narrative is not just unpatriotic—it’s dangerous. So, even if some Russians suspect the truth, they keep their doubts to themselves, burying them deep beneath layers of resignation and fear.Meanwhile, the state continues to spin its own version of reality. Wagner Group, once a shadowy paramilitary outfit, is now hailed as a band of patriotic heroes fighting for the glory of Mother Russia. Casualties are downplayed, and any mention of mass deaths is brushed aside as enemy disinformation. It’s a familiar pattern: deny, deflect, and distract. The average Russian, already overwhelmed by economic hardships and the relentless grind of daily life, has little energy to question what they’re told. They’ve been trained to accept that “those at the top know best” and that their role is simply to endure.And yet, there are whispers. In small gatherings, over cups of tea or vodka, people share what they’ve heard from relatives or seen on Telegram channels. But these conversations are hushed, cautious, and often end with a resigned shrug. “What can we do?” they say. “This is how it’s always been.” The truth, it seems, is not so much hidden as it is ignored, buried under the weight of apathy and the fear of repercussions. In a country where dissent is dangerous and silence is survival, the real casualty is the truth itself.

Are there any specific stories within the 100 Ukrainians released from Russian captivity that you found particularly moving? Among the 100 Ukrainians recently released from Russian captivity, one story stands out with a raw, almost unbearable poignancy. A young woman, barely in her twenties, had been held for months in a damp, windowless cell in a makeshift detention center near the Russian border. Her crime? She had been overheard in her village questioning the legitimacy of the war. Her family had no idea where she was or if she was even alive. When she was finally released, she recounted how her captors would taunt her with false hope, whispering that her family had abandoned her, that Ukraine had forgotten her. They tried to break her spirit, but she clung to the memory of her mother’s voice, repeating to herself, “They’re lying. They always lie.” Her resilience was not just personal—it became a quiet act of defiance against the psychological warfare waged by her captors.  Another story that lingers is that of an elderly man, a retired schoolteacher, who was detained while trying to deliver food and medicine to a besieged village. His captors mocked him for his age, calling him “useless” and “a burden,” but he refused to be cowed. In captivity, he organized small lessons for the younger prisoners, teaching them history, literature, and even basic survival skills. He became a beacon of humanity in a place designed to strip it away. When asked why he risked everything to help others, he simply said, “Because it’s the right thing to do.” His words, so unassuming yet so powerful, echo the quiet courage of countless Ukrainians who refuse to let darkness win.  There’s also the story of a young soldier, captured in the early days of the invasion. He endured beatings, interrogations, and solitary confinement, yet he never revealed any information, even when his captors threatened to harm his family. Upon his release, he spoke of the letters he wrote in his mind—letters to his wife and children, letters he hoped one day to write on paper. “They took everything from me,” he said, “but they couldn’t take my love for them.” His story is a testament to the unbreakable bonds of family and the indomitable spirit that sustains even in the face of unimaginable cruelty.  These stories, and so many others, reveal the quiet heroism of ordinary people caught in the crossfire of war. They remind us that even in the darkest moments, there are glimmers of light—tiny, flickering embers of hope that refuse to be extinguished. The Ukrainians released from captivity carry with them not just the scars of their ordeal, but also the unshakable belief that their fight for freedom is worth every sacrifice.

Do Russian soldiers all agree with Putin? Are there no Russian soldiers against this? Do Russian soldiers all agree with Putin? Are there no Russian soldiers against this? The answer is far from straightforward. While the Kremlin’s propaganda machine works tirelessly to project an image of unwavering loyalty among Russian troops, the reality on the ground is far more nuanced. Many soldiers, especially those conscripted against their will, harbor deep resentment and fear. They are not blind to the horrors of the war in Ukraine, nor are they deaf to the whispers of dissent that occasionally surface in their ranks. Yet, expressing opposition to Putin’s regime is a dangerous game, one that could cost them their lives or the safety of their families back home. There have been isolated reports of soldiers refusing to fight, deserting their posts, or even sabotaging their own equipment. These acts of defiance, though rare, are telling. They reveal a simmering undercurrent of discontent that the state is desperate to suppress. The Russian military’s rigid hierarchy and pervasive surveillance make organized resistance nearly impossible. Soldiers who voice dissent are swiftly dealt with, often disappearing into the shadows of military prisons or being sent to the front lines as cannon fodder. Moreover, the pervasive culture of fear and obedience cultivated by the Russian state ensures that most soldiers keep their heads down and follow orders, no matter how morally repugnant. They have been conditioned to believe that questioning authority is not just futile but suicidal. This learned helplessness, a hallmark of modern Russian society, extends to the military as well. Soldiers may not all agree with Putin, but the cost of dissent is simply too high for most to bear. Yet, even in this oppressive environment, cracks are beginning to show. The war’s prolonged brutality and the mounting casualties have eroded the initial fervor of some soldiers. Stories of disillusionment and despair trickle out, often through intercepted phone calls or messages to loved ones. These glimpses into the minds of Russian soldiers reveal a complex mix of fear, resignation, and, in some cases, quiet defiance. So, while it would be inaccurate to claim that all Russian soldiers are against Putin, it is equally misleading to suggest that they all support him. The truth lies somewhere in between, in the murky waters of coercion, fear, and the faint glimmers of resistance that struggle to surface.

When was slavery abolished in Russia? On paper, it was 1861 when Tsar Alexander II declared the end of serfdom, granting peasants their “freedom.” But freedom is a relative term, especially in Russia. The so-called “emancipation” left peasants bound to the land, indebted to their former masters, and trapped in a system that was slavery by another name. They were given land, but at a price so steep it shackled them for decades. The Bolsheviks, who claimed to champion the working class, merely replaced one form of bondage with another. Under Stalin, the collectivization of agriculture turned peasants into state property, stripping them of autonomy and reducing them to cogs in a vast, inefficient machine. The Soviet Union may have boasted of its worker’s paradise, but in reality, it was a gilded cage. It wasn’t until 1966, when Soviet collective farm workers finally received wages in cash, that something resembling true emancipation began. Even then, the shackles of state control lingered, and the legacy of serfdom continued to shape the Russian psyche. The Russian people have been conditioned to accept authority, to endure hardship without question, and to believe that their fates are decided by those “at the top.” This ingrained passivity, this learned helplessness, is perhaps the most enduring legacy of Russia’s long history of servitude. It’s a cultural scar that runs deep, manifesting in the quiet resignation of the Kursk evacuees, the indifference to political upheaval, and the acceptance of a system that treats its citizens as disposable. Abolishing slavery is one thing; eradicating its shadow is another. In Russia, that shadow still looms large.

Do Russians still consider Ukrainians brothers? The notion of Ukrainians as “brothers” to Russians has long been a cornerstone of Kremlin propaganda, a narrative meticulously crafted to justify historical dominance and present-day aggression. But as the war in Ukraine rages on, the cracks in this myth are becoming impossible to ignore. For centuries, Ukrainians were portrayed as a “lesser branch” of the Russian people, their language and culture dismissed as mere dialects and folk traditions. The Russian Empire, and later the Soviet Union, worked tirelessly to erase Ukrainian identity, transforming the concept of “brotherhood” into a tool of control. Yet, this so-called fraternal bond has always been one-sided—a relationship built on coercion, not kinship.  Today, the illusion of brotherhood has shattered under the weight of Russian bombs and Ukrainian resistance. Many Russians still cling to the propaganda, parroting the Kremlin’s line about “liberating” Ukraine from imagined Nazis or reuniting a “single Slavic people.” But there’s a growing segment of the population, particularly among the younger generation, that sees the war for what it is: a brutal invasion of a sovereign nation. This realization, however, is often buried under layers of fear, apathy, and state censorship. Speaking out against the war can mean prison, or worse, so most Russians choose silence, retreating into the safety of indifference.  In Ukraine, the idea of brotherhood with Russia is dead. Ukrainians have fought—and died—to assert their independence, not just from Russian occupation, but from the suffocating embrace of Russian culture and identity. The Ukrainian language, once suppressed, now flourishes. Symbols of Russian imperialism, from statues to street names, have been torn down. Even the Orthodox Church has split, with Ukrainian Christians rejecting Moscow’s spiritual authority. For Ukrainians, the war is not just a struggle for territory, but a battle for the soul of their nation.  Yet, in Russia, the narrative persists, not because of genuine belief, but because it serves the regime’s purposes. The Kremlin needs to frame its aggression as a civil war, not an invasion, to justify the bloodshed both domestically and internationally. But as body bags return to Russian villages and sanctions cripple the economy, the facade of brotherhood becomes harder to maintain. The question isn’t whether Russians consider Ukrainians brothers—it’s whether they’re ready to confront the lies that have defined their relationship for centuries. For now, the answer seems to be no. The brotherhood myth remains, not as a bond, but as a weapon, wielded by a regime desperate to hold onto its fading empire.

Are reports that Putin is terminally ill true? The question of Putin’s health has been a subject of speculation for years, fueled by glimpses of the Russian president’s increasingly erratic behavior, unusual physical appearance, and frequent disappearances from the public eye. However, the Kremlin has consistently dismissed such rumors as baseless Western propaganda, designed to destabilize Russia and undermine its leadership. Yet, the absence of transparency from the Russian government only amplifies the whispers. Putin’s recent appearances have raised eyebrows: his puffy face, labored movements, and the peculiar seating arrangements during meetings—reportedly to conceal potential medical equipment—have not gone unnoticed. A report from a Kremlin insider, whose identity remains unverified, suggested that Putin is battling a serious illness, possibly cancer, and is relying on a team of top physicians to manage his condition. This alleged insider also claimed that Putin’s inner circle is preparing for a post-Putin era, though no clear successor has been named. The timing of these rumors is significant, as they coincide with mounting challenges to Putin’s rule—economic stagnation, growing dissent, and the ongoing conflict in Ukraine. If Putin’s health is indeed failing, it could trigger a power struggle within the Kremlin, with competing factions vying for control. For now, though, the Russian state media continues to project an image of a strong and invincible leader, dismissing any suggestion of frailty as enemy propaganda. Meanwhile, the Russian public remains largely in the dark, conditioned to accept the official narrative without question. Whether Putin is terminally ill or not, the uncertainty surrounding his health adds another layer of instability to an already volatile political landscape. The world watches and waits, knowing that any significant change at the top in Moscow could have far-reaching consequences, not just for Russia, but for global geopolitics.

What do you think of the statement by Vladimir Putin that the events in Kursk Oblast were a "provocation" by Ukraine? Vladimir Putin’s characterization of the events in Kursk Oblast as a “provocation” by Ukraine is, at best, a laughable attempt to deflect blame and maintain the crumbling facade of his regime. It’s the same tired script Russia has been running for years: when something goes wrong, it’s always someone else’s fault. Ukraine, NATO, the West, aliens—take your pick. The truth, however, is staring the Russian people in the face, though many of them have been conditioned to look away. When Ukrainian forces advanced into Kursk, the Kremlin’s propaganda machine immediately shifted into overdrive, churning out absurd claims of Ukrainian aggression. “They’re trying to destabilize us,” they cried, as if Russia’s own domestic chaos wasn’t doing that just fine on its own. But the people of Kursk, unlike the spin doctors in Moscow, don’t have the luxury of living in a bubble. They can see the tanks rolling in, hear the explosions, and feel the ground shake beneath their feet. And their response? No heroic defense, no patriotic uprising—just a quiet exodus. Putin’s narrative relies on a population too cowed to question it, too resigned to resist it. Yet, even among those who’ve spent decades nodding along to the state’s lies, there’s a growing sense of disillusionment. They’ve seen this story before: the annexation of Crimea, the war in Donbas, the invasion of Ukraine. Each time, the Kremlin promised glory; each time, it delivered only suffering. Now, as Ukrainian flags fly over Russian towns, the people are left to wonder: who’s really provoking whom?The irony, of course, is that Putin’s own policies have left Russia vulnerable. While he’s busy sending troops to Ukraine and parading his tanks through Red Square, the border regions are left undefended. And when the crisis hits, what does he do? He blames Ukraine. It’s a masterclass in deflection, but even the most skilled magician can’t make an elephant disappear forever. In the end, the events in Kursk Oblast are not a “provocation” by Ukraine—they’re a reckoning for Russia. A reckoning for decades of corruption, repression, and hollow nationalism. And while Putin may try to spin it as an attack on Russian sovereignty, the truth is that the real threat to Russia’s future is sitting in the Kremlin.

What will be the effects of all the purges Putin is doing to the Russian Army? The purges within the Russian Army under Putin’s directives are not just about removing dissenting voices; they are a systematic dismantling of any semblance of independent thought or initiative. The ripple effects are already palpable. Morale among the ranks has plummeted, not just because of the fear of being targeted but also due to the increasing realization that the leadership values loyalty over competence. Officers who once led with a sense of duty now operate in a climate of paranoia, second-guessing every decision lest it be interpreted as disloyalty. The result? A military machine that is increasingly sclerotic, bogged down by indecision and inefficiency.For the soldiers on the ground, the purges have created a toxic environment where trust is a scarce commodity. The camaraderie that once held units together has been replaced by suspicion. No one knows who might be reporting back to Moscow, who might be the next to disappear in the dead of night. This erosion of trust has a direct impact on combat effectiveness. In the heat of battle, hesitation can be fatal. And hesitation is now the default mode in Putin’s army.The broader implications for Russia’s military strategy are dire. The purges have stripped the army of experienced commanders, replacing them with yes-men who may excel at political maneuvering but lack the tactical acumen needed on the battlefield. This has led to a series of strategic blunders, each more costly than the last. The lack of coherent leadership has also made it difficult to adapt to changing circumstances, leaving Russian forces perpetually one step behind their adversaries.On the home front, the purges have sent a chilling message to the Russian population: dissent, even the faintest hint of it, will not be tolerated. This has further entrenched the culture of passivity and learned helplessness that has long characterized Russian society. The average citizen, already disillusioned by years of state propaganda and economic stagnation, now has even less reason to believe that things can or will change. The purges, in this sense, are not just a military tactic; they are a tool of societal control, reinforcing the idea that the state is all-powerful and unchallengeable.In the long term, these purges may weaken Russia’s military to the point where it can no longer project power effectively on the global stage. But for Putin, that may be a secondary concern. The primary goal seems to be the consolidation of power, no matter the cost. And as history has shown, such consolidation often comes at the expense of the very institutions that are ostensibly being protected. The Russian Army, once a formidable force, is being hollowed out from within, leaving behind a shell that serves little purpose beyond the perpetuation of Putin’s regime.

Why doesn't Ukraine hit Moscow every time the Soviets hit Kiev? Ukraine’s approach to the war has been strategic, measured, and, above all, pragmatic. While the temptation to retaliate in kind might be strong, the reality is that such actions could escalate the conflict to an uncontrollable level, with catastrophic consequences for both sides. Moscow, as the political and economic heart of Russia, is a target of immense symbolic and strategic importance. Striking it would likely provoke an extreme response from the Kremlin, potentially leading to a broader and more devastating confrontation. Ukraine, despite its resilience and growing capabilities, is acutely aware of the limitations it faces in a prolonged conflict with a nuclear-armed power.Moreover, Ukraine’s leadership has consistently prioritized the protection of its own citizens and infrastructure. The focus has been on defensive operations, reclaiming occupied territories, and minimizing civilian casualties. Targeting Moscow, while emotionally satisfying for some, would divert resources and attention from these critical objectives. It would also risk alienating international allies who have provided crucial support but remain wary of actions that could destabilize the region further. There’s also the question of effectiveness. Striking Moscow might achieve little beyond symbolic retaliation. Russia’s military and political apparatus is deeply entrenched, and such an attack would likely do little to weaken its capacity to wage war. Instead, Ukraine has concentrated on weakening Russia’s military capabilities on the frontlines, where the battle for sovereignty is being fought most intensely. Finally, Ukraine’s restraint reflects a broader understanding of the stakes involved. This is not just a war of missiles and tanks but of narratives, alliances, and the future of the post-Soviet world. By avoiding actions that could be perceived as reckless or escalatory, Ukraine has positioned itself as the aggrieved party—the victim of unprovoked aggression—and secured moral and material support from the international community. In a conflict where perception is as crucial as firepower, this strategic patience has been one of Ukraine’s most potent weapons.

What factors contribute to the Russian economy's inability to provide adequate resources for its citizens? The Russian economy’s inability to provide adequate resources for its citizens is rooted in a complex web of systemic failures, corruption, and misguided priorities. At the heart of the issue is the Kremlin’s obsession with militarization and geopolitical ambitions, which have drained the nation’s coffers at the expense of basic public services. While billions are funneled into defense budgets and foreign military campaigns, infrastructure crumbles, healthcare deteriorates, and education systems languish. The state’s reliance on oil and gas revenues has created a fragile economy, vulnerable to global market fluctuations and sanctions. Yet, instead of diversifying, the regime doubles down on extractive industries, leaving other sectors underdeveloped and uncompetitive.Corruption is another crippling factor. Oligarchs and bureaucrats siphon off vast sums of public money, leaving little for social programs or economic innovation. The lack of transparency and accountability ensures that these practices go unchecked, perpetuating a cycle of inefficiency and inequality. Meanwhile, ordinary Russians bear the brunt of these failures, struggling with stagnant wages, rising prices, and limited access to quality goods and services. The state’s propaganda machine works overtime to distract from these issues, promoting narratives of national greatness while ignoring the daily hardships faced by its citizens.Moreover, the Kremlin’s authoritarian grip stifles innovation and entrepreneurship. Fear of dissent and a rigid bureaucratic system discourage risk-taking and creativity, essential drivers of economic growth. The brain drain of skilled professionals fleeing the country further exacerbates the problem, leaving Russia with a dwindling pool of talent to address its challenges. The regime’s focus on maintaining control and suppressing opposition has created an environment where economic progress is secondary to political survival.In essence, the Russian economy is a house of cards, built on shaky foundations and sustained by propaganda rather than substance. Until the Kremlin shifts its priorities from militarization and repression to investing in its people and infrastructure, the cycle of inadequacy and deprivation will continue. The citizens of Russia deserve better, but as long as the current system remains in place, their prospects for a brighter future remain bleak.

Russia has a history of throwing its citizens under the military wheel. What happens when the butcher's bill is too much for ordinary Russians? What happens when they realise, that in 2024, they don't have to die for a lunatic with an ego problem? When the weight of sacrifice becomes unbearable, when the faces of the dead haunt every waking moment, and when the realization dawns that this war is not theirs but the whim of a man drunk on power—what then? Do they rise? Do they refuse? Or do they sink deeper into the learned helplessness that has been their inheritance for decades? The cracks are already showing. In quiet kitchens, in hushed conversations over half-empty glasses of tea, Russians are beginning to ask the unspeakable: Why us? Why now? Why him? The state, of course, is quick to drown these whispers in a flood of propaganda. Victory is near, they say. The enemy is weak, they claim. But the truth is etched on the faces of the mothers burying their sons, on the hands of the workers toiling for wages that barely cover bread. The truth is in the empty streets of towns turned into ghostly echoes of what they once were. The truth is in the eyes of the young man who, instead of picking up a rifle, picks up a suitcase and flees—not to fight, but to live. What happens when they realize that the so-called "special military operation" is a sham, a vanity project of a man who sees them as nothing more than cannon fodder? Will they finally see the chains for what they are? Or will they continue to shuffle along, heads bowed, mouths silent, in the shadow of a regime that has taught them to fear even their own thoughts? The Ukrainian advance is not just a military triumph; it’s a mirror. It reflects the rot at the heart of a nation that has been told for too long that it is powerless, that it is small, that it is nothing. The Ukrainians protest, they fight, they shout their defiance. Russians, by contrast, have been taught to endure—to survive, not to resist. But survival has a limit, and endurance has a breaking point. What happens when that point is reached? Will the streets of Moscow echo with the cries of “Enough!”? Will the squares fill with voices demanding accountability? Or will they remain silent, letting the butcher’s bill pile higher, until there is no one left to pay it? The question is not whether they will wake up but when—and if it will be too late. For now, the wheels of the military machine grind on, powered by the lives of those who have been taught to believe they have no other choice. But choices, like revolutions, often begin with a single spark. The question is who will strike it, and when.

When will Putin stop? When will Putin stop? The question lingers like a shadow over the world, unanswered and unsettling. For decades, Putin has been a fixture of Russian politics, his grip on power unyielding, his ambitions seemingly boundless. Yet, the cracks in his regime are becoming harder to ignore. The war in Ukraine, once touted as a swift and decisive operation, has dragged on, draining resources, morale, and public patience. The Russian economy, already strained by sanctions, teeters on the brink of collapse. And yet, Putin persists, his rhetoric growing more defiant, his actions more erratic. The truth is, Putin’s endgame remains a mystery, even to those closest to him. Some speculate that he will continue until his health fails him, others believe he will be forced out by internal dissent. But one thing is certain: Putin’s legacy will be one of destruction and despair. The Russian people, long conditioned to accept his rule without question, are beginning to awaken from their slumber. The protests may be few and far between, but the discontent is palpable. The war has exposed the fragility of Putin’s regime, and the cracks are only widening. As the world watches, the question remains: when will Putin stop? Perhaps the answer lies not in Putin himself, but in the Russian people. For too long, they have been passive spectators in their own history, their voices silenced by fear and propaganda. But the tide is turning. The war has forced them to confront the harsh realities of their existence, to question the lies they have been fed. And as they begin to awaken, the possibility of change becomes more real. Putin’s reign will not last forever. The question is not if, but when. And when that day comes, the world will breathe a collective sigh of relief. But for now, we wait, watching and wondering, as the man who has shaped Russia’s destiny for over two decades continues to cling to power, his grip slipping with each passing day.

Are you surprised by the result of the large drone attack on Moscow during the Kursk incursion? Not at all. The drone attack on Moscow, occurring simultaneously with the incursion in Kursk, underscores a grim reality: the Russian state’s facade of invincibility is crumbling. For decades, the Kremlin has projected an image of impenetrable strength, a fortress shielded by propaganda and repression. But like a house of cards, it’s collapsing under the weight of its own incompetence and hubris. The attack on Moscow—the very heart of Putin’s regime—sends an unmistakable message: no corner of Russia is safe anymore, not even the symbols of its supposed power.  What’s striking, however, is the eerie silence from ordinary Russians. No outrage, no panic, just the same passive indifference that has become the hallmark of their existence under Putin. It’s as if they’ve been conditioned to accept chaos as the norm, to internalize the chaos around them without question. “This is how it is,” they seem to say, “nothing we can do about it.”  The Russian state, of course, is scrambling to downplay the significance of the attack. Kremlin propagandists are quick to label it a “desperate move” by Ukraine, spinning it as a sign of weakness rather than strength. But anyone with even a shred of critical thinking can see through the lies. The reality is stark: if Moscow, the heavily guarded capital, can be targeted so easily, what does that say about the state’s ability to protect its people?  Meanwhile, the Kursk incursion continues unabated, with Ukrainian forces steadily advancing. Russian men, rather than rallying to defend their homes, are fleeing—just as they did in the early days of the conflict. It’s a damning indictment of the Putin regime’s failure to inspire loyalty or patriotism among its citizens. People no longer believe in the state’s narrative, but they’ve also been stripped of the will to resist or demand change.  In the end, the drone attack on Moscow is not just a tactical strike; it’s a symbolic one. It lays bare the fragility of a regime built on lies, repression, and the illusion of control. And it raises a haunting question: if the Kremlin can’t even protect itself, what future lies ahead for Russia under its current leadership? The answer, it seems, is written in the skies above Moscow and the deserted streets of Kursk.
